candidate.answerReason: Each cube-root layer turns \(x\sqrt{x}\) back into \(\sqrt{x}\). The real domain is \(x\ge 0\).

methods.label: Recognize the same cube at each layer
methods.explanation:
The innermost square root requires \(x\ge 0\). The useful observation is that \(x\sqrt{x}\) is already a perfect cube:
\[
(\sqrt{x})^3=(\sqrt{x})^2\sqrt{x}=x\sqrt{x}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sqrt[3]{x\sqrt{x}}=\sqrt{x}.
\]
Starting at the innermost cube root, this identity replaces that entire layer by \(\sqrt{x}\). The middle layer then has the same form, and so does the outermost layer. Thus all three cube-root layers simplify in turn, leaving \(\boxed{\sqrt{x}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\). The argument includes \(x=0\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses square-root and cube-root definitions, with no fractional-exponent machinery.

candidate.annotationRationale: The simplification directly uses the inverse relationship between cubing and taking a cube root, together with \((\sqrt{x})^2=x\). The square-root domain is supporting knowledge. Fractional exponents are not assigned because the written method does not use them.
